costGuide.title: Mercedes-Benz M102 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an M102 engine typically takes 8-12 hours at £65-£85/hr (independent) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for this engine is the condition of the timing chain, valve stem seals, and the mechanical KE-Jetronic fuel injection system (on earlier models). Because the M102 is a classic Mercedes unit, recon specialists will typically strip the top end to replace all brittle plastic guides, fit new valve seals, and professionally refurbish the fuel distributor as standard. For a full breakdown of market rates, see our full reconditioned engine cost guide.

failures.title: Mercedes-Benz M102 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Stretch and Guide Wear - All variants
items.whatHappens: The plastic timing chain guide rails become brittle with age and heat, while the chain itself stretches. This leads to a distinct metallic rattling noise on cold starts. If ignored, the chain can jump a tooth, causing catastrophic valve-to-piston contact.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, a timing chain and guide kit replacement is straightforward and cost-effective. If valve damage has occurred, a full reconditioned M102 unit is required.

items.title: Valve Stem Seal Degradation - All variants
items.whatHappens: The original rubber valve stem seals harden and shrink over time, allowing oil to seep down the valve stems into the combustion chambers. This manifests as blue smoke from the exhaust on startup or after idling, accompanied by increased oil consumption.
items.repairVsReplace: This is a routine maintenance item, not a terminal failure. Replacing the valve stem seals is a standard, relatively inexpensive repair that restores clean operation.

items.title: KE-Jetronic Fuel Distributor Issues - Early SOHC variants
items.whatHappens: The mechanical continuous fuel injection system suffers from corroded control plungers, worn air flow sensor plates, and vacuum leaks. This leads to rough idling, poor fuel economy, and difficult cold starts.
items.repairVsReplace: Professional rebuilding or replacement of the fuel distributor is required. While the unit is rebuildable, sourcing a specialist to bench-test and calibrate it is essential.

failures.goodYearsLine: The M102 is widely regarded as one of Mercedes’ most robust inline-4 petrol engines ever built. Units maintained with regular oil changes and timely timing chain service routinely exceed 250,000 miles without major internal issues .

variants.title: M102 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: INTRO: The M102 family shares the same fundamental inline-4 block architecture, but displacement, cylinder head design (SOHC vs DOHC), and fuel delivery vary significantly. Identifying your exact sub-code is mandatory, as fitting the wrong revision can lead to severe mechanical incompatibility. - Fitted to: 190-Class W201 (190, 190E 2.0), E-Class W124 (200, 200E), C-Class W202 (C 180, early C 200) - Key technical difference: The base variant of the family, typically equipped with Bosch KE-Jetronic mechanical fuel injection and a single overhead camshaft. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; KE-Jetronic corrosion is the primary unique wear item. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with 2.3L variants due to different crankshafts, engine mounts, and ECU/fuel mapping. - Fitted to: E-Class W124 (230E), G-Class W460/W463 (230G, 230GE) - Key technical difference: Features a longer stroke for higher low-end torque. G-Class applications feature a ruggedised sump, revised oil pickup, and specific ancillary brackets for off-road use. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; G-Class variants may experience accelerated timing chain wear due to extreme operating angles. - Interchange note: Requires matching sump and oil pickup for G-Class applications; passenger car variants are not directly interchangeable with commercial/off-road specs without modification. - Fitted to: 190-Class W201 (190E 2.3-16), E-Class W124 (230E 2.3-16) - Key technical difference: Features a 16-valve cylinder head designed by Cosworth, higher compression ratio, dual overhead camshafts, and revised fuel mapping for high-performance applications. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; the higher-revving nature of the Cosworth head can accelerate valve guide wear if oil changes were neglected. - Interchange note: Not interchangeable with SOHC blocks without swapping the entire cylinder head, camshafts, pistons, and ECU/fuel system. - Fitted to: 190-Class W201 (190E 2.5-16, 190E 2.5-16 Evolution I/II), E-Class W124 (250E 2.5-16) - Key technical difference: Increased displacement to 2.5L, revised camshaft profiles, larger valves, and specific Evo-spec ancillary components for the homologation special models. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; rare and highly valuable, making preventative maintenance critical to preserve collector value. - Interchange note: Shares the DOHC architecture with the .960 but requires specific Evo-spec engine management, intake, and exhaust components to function correctly. ═══════════════════════════════════════ “# SECTION 7 - BUYING GUIDE: USED vs RECONDITIONED vs REBUILT ═══════════════════════════════════════ USED: A used M102 engine makes sense only if it comes with verifiable service history and documented proof of a recent timing chain and valve stem seal replacement. Given the age of these vehicles, buying a used unit with unknown history risks immediate, costly top-end repairs. RECONDITIONED: A proper reconditioned M102 engine is the sweet spot for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will proactively address the common failure points by fitting a new timing chain and plastic guides, replacing all valve stem seals, and professionally refurbishing the KE-Jetronic fuel distributor, giving the engine a fresh lease on life. REBUILT: A full M102 engine rebuild is highly justified for 190E 2.3-16 or 2.5-16 Evolution restorations where originality, matching numbers, and maximum longevity are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block, new pistons/rings, and a balanced crankshaft. SUPPLY & FIT LINE: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your M102 engine is installed by specialists familiar with classic Mercedes mechanical and KE-Jetronic systems, backed by a nationwide warranty. VEHICLE VALUE NOTE: Because the M102 is typically found in W201, W124, and W463 vehicles valued between £2,000 and £15,000+ (with 2.5-16 Evolution models commanding significantly higher premiums), a full replacement is generally financially viable. However, if the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing .

items.question: How much does a Mercedes M102 engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes M102 engine typically costs between £1,200 and £2,200 for supply only . Fitted costs generally range from £1,800 to £3,000 depending on the specialist, while used units can be found from £400 but carry a high financial risk due to the engine's age and brittle plastic components. items.question: What is the most common failure on the M102 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are timing chain stretch and plastic guide rail wear, valve stem seal degradation causing blue smoke, and KE-Jetronic fuel distributor corrosion. The timing chain guides become brittle with age and can cause catastrophic valve damage if the chain jumps, while valve stem seals are a routine but labour-intensive maintenance item. Get quotes for a rebuilt M102 with these issues resolved

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the M102 engine?
items.answer: The M102 was fitted to the W201 190-Class (190, 190E, 190E 2.3-16, 190E 2.5-16), the W124 E-Class (200E, 230E, 230E 16V), the W460/W463 G-Class (230G, 230GE), and the early W202 C-Class (C 180, C 200), serving as the definitive 4-cylinder petrol for these chassis between 1982 and 1996. items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned M102 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned M102 is strongly recommended over a used unit. A proper rebuild will proactively address the fatal flaws of age by fitting a new timing chain and updated plastic guides, replacing all hardened valve stem seals, and professionally refurbishing the KE-Jetronic fuel distributor, whereas a used engine with unknown history risks immediate top-end repairs. items.question: What is the difference between M102.920, .940, .960, and .980?
items.answer: The M102.920 is the 2.0L SOHC variant, the .940 is the 2.3L SOHC variant, the .960 is the 2.3L DOHC 16-valve Cosworth variant, and the .980 is the 2.5L DOHC 16-valve Cosworth Evolution variant. They share the same core block, but the cylinder heads, camshafts, and fuel mapping differ significantly, making the high-revving Cosworth variants highly collectable and non-interchangeable with the SOHC blocks.
